summary: Requires that TLS clients and servers never negotiate SSL version 2.0, because it is known to be insecure. It updates the backward compatibility sections of RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and RFC 5246. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: SSL version 2.0 is an old way to secure a connection that has several known weaknesses. This document requires modern clients and servers to refuse to use it, even though a server may still recognize its old-style greeting and reject it.

questions: how do tls clients avoid ssl 2.0
what versions can tls servers accept
subtitle: Requires TLS clients and servers never to negotiate the insecure SSL version 2.0.

tldr.problem: Some TLS clients and servers still supported negotiating SSL version 2.0, which has known deficiencies and does not give a sufficiently high level of security.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates the backward compatibility sections of TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2: clients MUST NOT send an SSL 2.0 compatible CLIENT-HELLO, and servers MUST NOT reply with an SSL 2.0 SERVER-HELLO.
tldr.outcome: SSL 2.0 may never be negotiated. The RFC is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists RFC 8996 as updating it.

today: RFC 6176 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and RFC 5246. The unit metadata lists RFC 8996 as updating it.

sections.title: Why SSL 2.0 Goes
sections.content:
Many protocols specified in the IETF rely on Transport Layer Security (TLS) for security services, but some TLS clients and servers also support negotiating SSL version 2.0, which has known deficiencies. This document requires that TLS clients and servers never negotiate it.

RFC 4346 and later RFC 5246 had warned that the ability to send version 2.0 CLIENT-HELLO messages "will be phased out with all due haste". RFC 6176 does this by updating the backward compatibility sections of RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and RFC 5246.
sections.plainLanguage: Older TLS rule books warned that the old SSL 2.0 greeting would be removed soon. This document does it now by changing the compatibility rules in those earlier specifications.

sections.title: The SSL 2.0 Deficiencies
sections.content:
The RFC lists four problems with SSL version 2.0:

  • Message authentication uses MD5, which most security-aware users have already moved away from.
  • Handshake messages are not protected, so a man-in-the-middle can trick the client into picking a weaker cipher suite than it would normally choose.
  • Message integrity and message encryption use the same key, which is a problem if the client and server negotiate a weak encryption algorithm.
  • Sessions can be easily terminated: a man-in-the-middle can insert a TCP FIN, and the peer cannot tell whether it was a legitimate end of the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The old protocol has four flaws: it authenticates with a weak hash, leaves the negotiation open to tampering, uses one key for two jobs, and lets an outsider end the session without the other side noticing.

sections.title: What TLS Implementations Must Do
sections.content:
TLS clients MUST NOT send the SSL version 2.0 compatible CLIENT-HELLO message format, and MUST NOT send any ClientHello specifying a protocol version less than { 0x03, 0x00 }. A client SHOULD specify the highest protocol version it supports.

TLS servers MAY continue to accept ClientHello messages in the version 2 CLIENT-HELLO format described in RFC 5246, Appendix E.2, which does not contradict the ban on negotiating SSL 2.0. Servers MUST NOT reply with an SSL 2.0 SERVER-HELLO at a version below { 0x03, 0x00 }, and instead MUST abort the connection, so a client whose highest offered version is { 0x02, 0x00 } is refused.
sections.plainLanguage: A client must not offer a protocol version older than 3.0, and it should offer the newest it knows. A server may still read the old greeting format, but it must not answer at an old version; it must close the connection instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the entire document is about security considerations. It adds that the number of servers supporting the optional acceptance of the version 2 CLIENT-HELLO is declining, and that this greeting format precludes the use of TLS protocol enhancements that require TLS extensions, since extensions can only be sent in an (Extended) ClientHello handshake message.
sections.plainLanguage: The document exists to remove an insecure option. It also notes that the old greeting cannot carry newer TLS extensions, so keeping it would block useful improvements.
